lesson.title: Seven Debates That Made a President: Lincoln and Douglas in 1858
lesson.summary: In their 1858 race for an Illinois Senate seat, Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas held seven public debates over slavery's expansion that made Lincoln a national figure and helped split the Democratic Party in two.
lesson.body:
In 1858, Stephen Douglas, the incumbent Democratic senator from Illinois, faced a serious challenge for reelection from Abraham Lincoln, a former one term congressman running as the candidate of the new Republican Party. Because state legislatures, not ordinary voters, elected United States senators at the time, the real contest was over which party would control the Illinois legislature, but Lincoln and Douglas campaigned across the state almost as if voters were choosing between them directly, agreeing to meet in seven joint debates held in different congressional districts.

Lincoln opened the campaign with a speech in Springfield on June 16, 1858, accepting the Republican nomination, in which he warned that the country could not endure permanently half slave and half free, and that the nation's house divided against itself would eventually become all one thing or all the other. The line, borrowed loosely from scripture, framed the entire campaign around the stakes of slavery's expansion rather than any narrower local issue, and it built directly on the argument the young Republican Party had been making since its founding in 1854.

Between August and October 1858, Lincoln and Douglas held seven debates in the towns of Ottawa, Freeport, Jonesboro, Charleston, Galesburg, Quincy, and Alton. Crowds numbering in the thousands, sometimes tens of thousands, gathered to watch, and newspapers across the state and beyond published lengthy transcripts, turning a state legislative race into a debate followed by a national audience.

The debates circled constantly back to the Dred Scott decision and what it meant for popular sovereignty, the idea Douglas had championed in the Kansas Nebraska Act that territorial settlers should decide slavery's fate for themselves. At the second debate, in Freeport, Lincoln pressed Douglas on whether a territory could still lawfully exclude slavery given the Supreme Court's ruling that Congress had no power to ban it there. Douglas answered that slavery could not actually take root anywhere local settlers refused to pass the police regulations and slave codes needed to support it in practice, so a territory could exclude slavery in effect simply by declining to protect it, an answer that became known as the Freeport Doctrine.

Douglas's answer helped him at home. The Democrats held onto control of the Illinois legislature, thanks partly to district lines drawn after the 1850 census that favored Democratic areas, and lawmakers reelected Douglas to the Senate. But the Freeport Doctrine badly damaged Douglas nationally, since southern Democrats wanted the federal government to actively protect slavery in the territories and saw his answer as a betrayal, a split that would help break the Democratic Party into rival northern and southern factions in the 1860 election. Lincoln, despite losing the Senate race, emerged from the widely reprinted debates as one of the most recognized Republicans in the country, positioning him for the party's presidential nomination just two years later.
